title: American Sign Language is closer to French signing than to British
body: Sign languages are not universal, and they don’t follow the spoken language around them. American Sign Language grew up at the American School for the Deaf, founded in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1817 by Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc, a deaf teacher from France who taught in French Sign Language. Pupils blended Clerc’s signs with local sign languages, including Martha’s Vineyard’s, and a new language emerged. Today about **58 per cent of ASL signs** are cognates of old French signs, while ASL and British Sign Language are mutually unintelligible.

left.label: ASL and BSL
left.text: Not mutually intelligible, even though both communities read and write English.

right.label: ASL and LSF
right.text: Closest relatives: about 58% of modern ASL signs are cognates of Old French Sign Language signs.

events.text: Gallaudet and Clerc open the American School for the Deaf
Pupils from Martha’s Vineyard bring their island’s sign language
Estimates of ASL users in the US run from 250,000 to 500,000

slides.label: sign languages officially recognised around the world
slides.text: ASL users have never been counted by the US census, so even its own numbers are estimates.

slides.heading: A creole?
slides.text: Some linguists have proposed that ASL is a creole of French Sign Language, born when Clerc’s signs met the signing that deaf pupils brought from home. The 58% figure is well below the 80% usually expected between dialects of one language, so ASL counts as a language of its own.

slides.question: Where did American Sign Language emerge?
options: American School for the Deaf, Hartford
slides.explanation: At the school Gallaudet and Clerc opened in Hartford in 1817, where Clerc’s French signs blended with the sign languages pupils brought with them, including Martha’s Vineyard’s.
